explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Welcome back to Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. By now you know that this subject is not about memorising facts. It is about growing a set of thinking skills you can use for the rest of your life, in any subject and in the real world around you.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you are building all of them, one unit at a time:

This unit is about the third skill: Evaluation. In Research you learned to find information. In Analysis you learned to break a topic apart and ask why. Now you will learn to judge what you find: is this source trustworthy, is this argument strong, and how much should I believe it? Evaluation is the skill that protects you from being fooled.

You may wonder why evaluation matters beyond school. Think about how much information reaches you every day: messages forwarded on a phone, videos, adverts, things friends repeat as if they were true. Some of it is honest and careful. Some of it is exaggerated, one-sided, or simply invented to sell something or to stir people up. The person who can tell the difference makes better choices, wastes less money, and is much harder to trick. That is a skill worth having for life.
bullets: Research — finding out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — breaking a topic into parts and asking why things happen.
Evaluation — deciding how strong and how trustworthy an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking about how you learn and how you have changed your mind.
Collaboration — working well with other people.
Communication — sharing your ideas clearly so others understand you.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning in Ehel Academy's self-paced way, which means three kinds of support work together:

In the old style of this subject, learners were told to 'discuss with a partner' or 'share with the class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. Evaluation is a skill you sharpen by arguing your judgement out loud and letting someone question it. So every time you see an 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box, treat it as a real debate. Say what you think, give your reasons, and let the tutor test them.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete the activities in your own time. You can slow down on a hard idea or move quickly through an easy one.

Your AI tutor, available 24 hours a day. Whenever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a study partner and a whole class of classmates in one. It will discuss your judgements, push back on weak reasons, and give you feedback at any hour.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In your live sessions you share your best thinking, ask the questions that matter most, and hear how other learners judged the same source differently.

explainers.title: Meet Tariq, our evaluator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make each part of evaluation clear, we will follow one Year 7 learner all the way through the unit. His name is Tariq, and he is a student at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

Lately, Tariq keeps seeing strong, contradictory messages about mobile phones and social media. One post, forwarded many times, claims that phones make young people fail every exam. Another, an advert, claims a new study app 'guarantees top marks in two weeks'. His friends repeat both as if they were obviously true, even though they cannot both be right. Tariq starts to wonder: which of these sources can I actually trust, and how do I decide what to believe?

That question becomes Tariq's project for this unit. As you meet each part of evaluation, you will see exactly what Tariq does with it: how he tests whether a source is real, spots who is trying to sell him something, separates fact from opinion, and finally decides which argument about phones is stronger, and why. You will be doing the very same thing with sources about a topic that matters to you.

explainers.title: Your Challenge continues
explainers.body:
In Research you chose a Challenge: a global topic that also matters right where you live. In this unit your Challenge grows. Instead of only gathering information about it, you will now evaluate the information and the arguments people make about it.

If you already have a Challenge topic from earlier units, keep it. If you are joining now, choose one of these arguable topics, or one of your own. Notice that each one is worded as a question people genuinely disagree about, because evaluation needs at least two sides to weigh:

You do not have to decide your final answer yet. That is the whole point. A good evaluator holds back their judgement until they have weighed the sources and arguments on both sides. Keep a note of any claim about your topic that made you think 'is that really true?' Those doubts are the seeds of good evaluation.
bullets: Should students our age use smartphones and social media?
Should our town ban thin plastic bags?
Is bottled water really safer than water from a protected well?
Should our school day start later in the morning?
Are solar lamps a better choice for families than the mains supply?
Should street food sellers follow stricter hygiene rules?
Is it fair to keep animals such as birds and fish as pets?

explainers.title: What is evaluation, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think being 'critical' just means saying you do not like something. Real evaluation is more careful and more fair than that. Evaluation is judging how trustworthy a source is and how strong an argument is, by weighing its strengths and its weaknesses, and then reaching a judgement you can support with reasons.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, an evaluator always looks for both strengths and weaknesses, never only the faults. Second, an evaluator gives reasons for every judgement, so it is never just 'I think it is bad', but 'I think it is weak because ...'. A judgement without a reason is only an opinion.

explainers.title: Evaluation and analysis: what is the difference?
explainers.body:
Evaluation and analysis are close cousins, and learners often mix them up. Here is the difference in one line. Analysis breaks a topic apart and asks why things happen. Evaluation judges how good, strong or trustworthy something is. Analysis explains; evaluation judges.

A quick test is to look for the words a sentence uses. Evaluation sentences usually contain judging words such as strength, weakness, reliable, convincing, or better. Analysis sentences usually contain explaining words such as because, reason, cause, or this leads to.

explainers.title: Judging a source: is it real or fake? (Objective 3.1)
explainers.body:
The first big part of evaluation is judging an information source: a website, a news story, a message, a video. Not everything that looks like news really is. Fake news is a story that is invented or twisted, but dressed up to look like a real report so that people share it and believe it.

Fake news exists for reasons, and knowing them helps you spot it. Some is made to earn money from clicks and adverts. Some is made to sell a product. Some is made to make people angry, or to make one group look bad. A lot of it spreads on social media, where anyone can post anything and a dramatic story travels fast before anyone checks it.

explainers.title: The reliability checklist (Objective 3.1)
explainers.body: To judge a source fairly instead of by feeling alone, evaluators use a checklist. Work through these questions for any source. The more you answer 'yes' to, the more reliable the source probably is. A reliable source is one that can be trusted to be true; an unreliable source is one that cannot.
bullets: Has the story been reported anywhere else?
Is it also on the radio, TV or in well-known newspapers?
Have you heard of the author or the organisation that published it?
Does the website itself look real and professional?
Does the web address at the very top of the page look real?
Does the story sound believable, or is it wildly dramatic?
Are there spelling or grammar mistakes?
Is the author a real, named person you can find out about?
Is there anything odd about the dates?
Is there any other evidence that supports the story?

explainers.title: Author and purpose: who made this, and why? (Objective 3.1)
explainers.body:
Cambridge asks you to evaluate a source by considering its author and its purpose. Every source is made by someone, for a reason. Once you know who made it and why, you can judge how much to trust it.

Purposes vary. A source might exist to inform you honestly, to persuade you to agree, to sell you something, or to entertain you. A source that mainly wants to sell or persuade is not automatically false, but it has a reason to show only one side, so you should read it more carefully.

explainers.title: Fact and opinion: telling them apart (Objective 3.1)
explainers.body:
Sources mix two very different things, and a strong evaluator keeps them separate. A fact is something that can be checked and proven to be true. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others could reasonably disagree with.

Opinions are not bad. A strong argument often includes them. But you must know which is which, because a source that hides an opinion inside factual-sounding words is trying, perhaps without meaning to, to slip a judgement past you.
bullets: Fact: 'In the dry season, some families in Hargeisa walk more than twenty minutes to collect water.' This can be checked.
Opinion: 'Collecting water is the worst part of the dry season.' This is a feeling; another person might disagree.

explainers.title: Spotting bias, exaggeration and unsupported claims (Objective 3.1)
explainers.body:
Bias is when a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced. It is a judgement based on a personal point of view, a kind of favouring one side or being prejudiced for or against something. A source with a vested interest is often biased, because it has a reason to show only the good or only the bad.

Two close relatives of bias are worth naming. Exaggeration is stretching the truth to make it sound bigger or worse than it is, such as 'phones destroy every single child's brain'. An unsupported claim is a statement given with no evidence at all, such as 'everyone knows this is the best'. Both are signals to slow down and ask for proof.

explainers.title: What is an argument? (Objective 3.2)
explainers.body:
Evaluation is not only about single sources; it is also about arguments. In Global Perspectives, an argument does not mean a quarrel or shouting. An argument is a claim, plus the reasons for that claim, plus the evidence that supports it. Those three parts are what you look for and what you judge.

A simple way to remember the three parts is to ask three questions:

A strong argument has all three, and the evidence really does support the claim. A weak argument is missing a part, usually the evidence, or offers evidence that does not actually fit the claim.
bullets: The claim answers: What do I think?
The reason answers: Why do I think this?
The evidence answers: How do I know this?

explainers.title: Claims, and how to test them (Objective 3.2)
explainers.body:
The heart of any argument is its claim: the thing the author wants you to accept. A good claim is debatable, which means sensible people could disagree with it. 'Water is wet' is not a claim, because nobody argues about it. 'Our town should ban plastic bags' is a claim, because people take different sides.

A quick way to write or spot a claim is to start with the words 'The author believes ...' or 'I believe ...'. Whatever comes next is the claim.

Once you have found a claim, you test it. Testing a claim means checking it against evidence and against what other people think, to see whether it holds up. You do this by asking sharp questions such as: What evidence is there? Who might disagree, and why? Is there another explanation?

explainers.title: Evidence: numerical and narrative (Objective 3.2)
explainers.body:
A claim is only as strong as its evidence. Evidence is anything that can back up a claim, such as a survey result, a report or a study. In this context, useful evidence must also be relevant, meaning it is genuinely related to the claim being made, not just interesting.

Evidence comes in two helpful types, and strong arguments often use both:

Numbers show how widespread something is; narratives show what it feels like and why. An argument backed by both a clear number and a real story is usually more convincing than one with only one type.
bullets: Numerical evidence comes from closed questions that give numbers, such as a yes or no answer or a choice from a list. Example: '80 out of 100 students own a phone.'
Narrative evidence comes from open questions, often 'why' questions, that give a fuller story in someone's own words. Example: a student explaining why her phone helps her study at night.

explainers.title: Judging how strong an argument is (Objective 3.2)
explainers.body:
Now you can judge a whole argument, not just its parts. To evaluate an argument, you weigh its strengths and its weaknesses, exactly as Cambridge asks. You are deciding how effective and convincing it is.

Here are questions that reveal an argument's strengths and weaknesses:

A fair evaluation names at least one strength and at least one weakness, and then reaches an overall judgement. Even a weak argument usually has one strength, and even a strong one usually has a weakness. Finding both is what makes your evaluation trustworthy.
bullets: Does it have a clear claim, real reasons and relevant evidence?
Is the evidence reliable, and does it actually support the claim?
Does it deal fairly with the other side, or ignore it?
Is anything exaggerated, biased, or claimed with no support?

explainers.title: Comparing two arguments (Objectives 3.1 and 3.2)
explainers.body:
The most useful evaluation of all is comparing two arguments on opposite sides of a question and deciding which is stronger. This brings every skill in this unit together: you judge each source, weigh each argument's strengths and weaknesses, and then compare them fairly.

To compare fairly, judge both arguments by the same questions. Do not be tougher on the side you already disagree with. Line them up, strength against strength and weakness against weakness, and see which one truly stands up better.

explainers.title: Making and justifying your judgement
explainers.body:
Evaluation always ends in a judgement: a clear decision about how much to trust a source, or which argument is stronger. But a judgement on its own is not enough. You must justify it, which means giving the reasons and evidence that led you there.

A well-justified judgement usually follows this shape: state your decision, give your main reason, point to the evidence, and honestly note the strongest point on the other side. Admitting the other side's best point does not weaken you; it shows you judged fairly.

explainers.title: How evaluation connects to the other skills
explainers.body:
Evaluation sits in the middle of the six skills, and it links to all of them.

So evaluation is not a step you finish and leave behind. It is a habit of mind you carry into every other skill, and into every choice you make with information.
bullets: Research gives you the sources; evaluation decides which ones deserve your trust.
Analysis breaks a topic into parts; evaluation then judges which parts and arguments are strong.
Reflection grows every time you notice a source that changed your mind, or a judgement you got wrong at first.
Collaboration works better when you can weigh a partner's idea fairly, praising its strengths and naming its weaknesses kindly.
Communication becomes powerful when you back your message with well-judged sources instead of weak ones.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the evaluation cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every part of evaluation in this unit. Here is how they fit into one smooth cycle you can use for any source or argument:
bullets: Check the source: is it real or fake? Run the reliability checklist.
Consider the author and purpose, and watch for a vested interest.
Separate the facts from the opinions.
Spot any bias, exaggeration or unsupported claims.
Find the argument: name the claim, the reasons and the evidence.
Weigh the strengths and weaknesses, and compare the two sides fairly.
Reach a judgement, and justify it with reasons and evidence.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Reflection. Once you can judge sources and arguments, reflection teaches you to turn that judging inward: to think about how you learn, how your mind has changed, and how you can improve. Strong evaluation now will make strong reflection much easier later. Well done for building a skill that will keep you from being fooled for the rest of your life.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to remember
lines: Evaluation is not about finding information; it is about judging it.
A researcher asks: can I find something out? An evaluator asks: can I trust it, and how strong is it?

As always in Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle and the skill is the destination. We will judge sources about phones, water and plastic, but the point is to become someone who can weigh almost any claim fairly.

bigIdeas.title: Warning signs that something might be fake
lines: You have never heard of the website or the person who published it.
The story is dramatic or shocking, and it is designed to make you feel strong emotions quickly.
It offers something that seems too good to be true, such as free prizes or a guaranteed result.
No other trusted source, such as the radio, TV or well-known newspapers, is reporting it.
There are spelling or grammar mistakes, no author's name, or something odd about the dates.

bigIdeas.title: A useful rule of thumb
lines: It is most likely that you will already have heard of the more reliable sources of information.
Big, trusted organisations have a reputation to protect, so they usually check a story before publishing it.
If a shocking story appears only on a website nobody has ever heard of, that is a reason to be careful, not a reason to share.
Try searching for the author's name to see who they are and what else they have written.

bigIdeas.title: Watch for a vested interest
lines: A vested interest is when the person or group behind a source has something to gain from you believing it.
A company selling a product has a vested interest in telling you the product is wonderful.
This does not prove they are lying, but it means their source is not a fair, balanced judge.
When you spot a vested interest, look for a second source that has nothing to gain, to balance it.

bigIdeas.title: A fairness note for Global Perspectives
lines: Imagine a community question that Muslim and Christian families might see differently, such as which holidays a shared calendar should include.
A biased source quotes only one group and calls the other group unreasonable.
A fair source explains both viewpoints evenly and lets you weigh them yourself.
Being fair does not mean having no view. It means forming your view only after listening to every side, which is the heart of Global Perspectives.

bigIdeas.title: Reliable and unreliable, in one line
lines: A reliable source can be trusted to be true.
An unreliable source cannot be trusted to be true.
A vested interest does not prove a source is wrong, but it means the source is not a fair, balanced judge.
When you spot a vested interest, find a second source with nothing to gain, to balance it.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Use the same Challenge topic you have been exploring, worded as a question with two sides.
In every activity you will judge real-ish sources and arguments about it.
By the end you will have a justified judgement you can share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: The source to judge
lines: A brightly coloured website you have never heard of posts a shocking headline: 'Miracle drink cures every illness in one day!'
There is no author's name and no date. The web address has odd extra words in it.
No newspaper, radio or TV station is reporting the story. There are several spelling mistakes.
The page ends by asking you to pay money to receive the drink 'before it sells out'.

bigIdeas.title: The passage to judge
lines: Everybody knows that plastic bags are completely destroying our beautiful town. They are the single worst thing on the planet, and only a foolish person would ever defend them.
Our brilliant clean-up group is the only group that truly cares. No sensible reason exists to keep using bags, and anyone who disagrees simply has not thought about it.

bigIdeas.title: The passage
lines: Our school should provide free drinking water at every classroom. Students would concentrate better in the afternoon heat, because a recent school survey found that two out of three students said they feel thirsty and tired by the last lesson of the day.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a claim worth testing
lines: It is debatable, so sensible people could take different sides.
It is clear, so everyone understands exactly what is being claimed.
It is about your topic, not a side issue.
It can be checked against real evidence, not just feelings.

bigIdeas.title: Keep your comparison fair
lines: Judge both arguments by the same set of questions.
Do not be harder on the side you already disagree with.
Look for at least one strength and one weakness in each.
End with a judgement that rests on a reason, not just a feeling.

models.title: Evaluation happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine two sellers in the market each promise their phone charger is 'the best'.
You do not just believe the loudest one. You weigh strengths and weaknesses: one charger has a guarantee but costs more; the other is cheap but you have never heard of the brand.
You ask who is telling you this and why: both sellers want your money, so you also ask a friend who already owns one.
You reach a judgement with a reason: I will buy the guaranteed one, because a guarantee is worth the extra cost. That is evaluation, and you already do it.

So evaluation is not a strange school-only activity. It is the honest weighing you already do before you trust a seller, a rumour or a promise. In this unit you will simply learn to do it on purpose, with more skill, and about sources that matter.

models.title: Analysis or evaluation? Tariq sorts some sentences
lines: A. One strength is that the writer listens to other people's views. -> Evaluation (it judges a strength).
B. One reason for the flooding is the continued dumping of plastic in the drains. -> Analysis (it explains a cause).
C. Its only weakness is that the information is ten years out of date. -> Evaluation (it judges a weakness).
D. This is happening because of the ever-increasing number of cars in the city. -> Analysis (it explains why).
E. The argument is not convincing, because it gives no evidence. -> Evaluation (it judges, and gives a reason).
Notice sentence E: it does both jobs well. It reaches a judgement (not convincing) and gives a reason (no evidence). That is the shape of strong evaluation you are aiming for all through this unit.

models.title: Zara's example: the sea turned red
lines: Zara sees a forwarded post claiming the sea near Berbera turned bright red overnight, with a blurry photo.
She has never heard of the website. No Hargeisa or Mogadishu radio station, TV channel or newspaper is reporting it. There is no author and no date.
The story is dramatic and made her gasp, which is exactly what a fake story is designed to do.
Zara decides not to share it until a source she trusts confirms it. Later, nothing does, and she is glad she waited.
The habit to build is simple: before you believe or share, pause and check. A true story will still be true in an hour, so there is never any harm in slowing down to evaluate it first.

models.title: Tariq runs the checklist on the study-app advert
lines: The 'guaranteed top marks' advert is on a website Tariq has never heard of. No newspaper or school mentions it.
There is no named author, the dates are missing, and there are two spelling mistakes.
The only 'evidence' is a single glowing review with no name attached.
Almost every checklist answer is 'no'. Tariq judges the source unreliable and does not spend his money.

models.title: Karim's example: two leaflets about plastic bags
lines: Karim finds two leaflets about banning thin plastic bags in his town on the Horn of Africa coast.
One is from a company that makes plastic bags. Its purpose is to persuade people to keep using them. That is a vested interest.
The other is from a volunteer beach clean-up group led by Amara Diallo, with no product to sell. Its purpose is to inform people about litter.
Karim does not throw the first leaflet away, but he trusts it less, because the makers gain if bags are not banned.

models.title: Nadia's example: a paragraph about school meals
lines: Nadia reads: 'The school serves rice four days a week. This is clearly a terrible diet, and everyone knows fruit is the only healthy food.'
Fact: the school serves rice four days a week. That can be checked.
Opinion: the diet is 'terrible' and fruit is 'the only healthy food'. Those are judgements, not proven facts.
Spotting the mix, Nadia trusts the fact but tests the opinion against other sources before she accepts it.

models.title: Omar's example: a solar-lamp advert
lines: Omar reads an advert that says: 'Our solar lamp is the best in the whole world. Everyone agrees. Buy it today before it is too late!'
Bias: it is made by the seller, who favours their own product.
Exaggeration: 'the best in the whole world' stretches the truth.
Unsupported claim: 'everyone agrees' is given with no evidence. Omar looks for an independent review before deciding.

models.title: Layla's example: finding the three parts
lines: Layla reads: 'Our school should start later. Students would learn more, because research shows teenagers who sleep longer concentrate better in class.'
Claim: the school should start later.
Reason: students would learn more.
Evidence: research showing that teenagers who sleep longer concentrate better. All three parts are present, so this is a reasonably strong argument.

models.title: Tariq's example: testing a claim about phones
lines: Claim from a post: 'Phones make young people fail every exam.'
Tariq rewrites it clearly: the author believes phones cause exam failure.
He tests it with questions: Where is the evidence? Do some students with phones still do well? Could other things, such as not sleeping, be the real cause?
The claim is an exaggeration that ignores other causes, so Tariq judges it weak, even though phones can be a distraction.

models.title: Tariq's example: two kinds of evidence about phones
lines: Tariq runs a small survey. A closed question gives numerical evidence: 18 of 25 classmates use a phone to study at least once a week.
An open question gives narrative evidence: one classmate explains that she reads lessons on her phone after dark because there is no other light.
Together, the number and the story make a far stronger case than either alone.

models.title: Dina's example: weighing one argument
lines: Argument: 'Our school should ban fizzy drinks, because a school survey found most students feel tired after drinking them.'
Strength: it has a clear claim and offers evidence from a survey.
Weakness: 'feeling tired' is an opinion the students reported, not a proven medical fact, and no other side is considered.
Dina's judgement: a fair start, but not yet convincing, because the evidence is thin and one-sided.

models.title: Tariq's example: two articles about phones for students
lines: Article A, from a company that sells phones, argues students should all have phones. Strength: it gives a real example of a pupil learning online. Weakness: it has a vested interest and ignores any downside.

Article B, a children's-charity report by Dr Amina Kapoor with nothing to sell, argues for limits on phone use. Strength: it uses a survey and admits phones have some benefits. Weakness: its survey was quite small.
Comparing them by the same questions, Tariq judges Article B stronger: it uses evidence, deals fairly with both sides, and has no vested interest, even though its evidence is not perfect.

models.title: Tariq's justified judgement about phones
lines: Judgement: I think the argument for sensible limits on phone use is stronger than the claim that phones ruin every student.
Reason and evidence: the stronger source uses a survey, has no vested interest, and deals fairly with both sides.
Fair note: I accept that phones can genuinely help students who study online after dark, so limits should be sensible, not a total ban.
That is a judgement Tariq can defend, because every part of it rests on a reason.

models.title: Tariq's whole journey, from confusion to judgement
lines: He learned that a source can look like news but be fake, and ran the reliability checklist on the study-app advert.
He asked who wrote each source and why, and spotted a vested interest in the sellers.
He separated fact from opinion, and named the bias and exaggeration in the loudest posts.
He found the claims, reasons and evidence in two opposing articles about phones.
He weighed each argument's strengths and weaknesses and compared them by the same questions.
He reached a justified judgement he can defend, and he stayed fair to the other side.

By following this cycle, Tariq turned a confusing storm of online claims into a calm, well-reasoned judgement. In the Activities file, you will run the same cycle on sources about your own Challenge topic, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Challenge question: Should students our age use smartphones and social media?
Yes side: phones help students learn, stay safe and keep in touch.
No side: phones distract students, cost money and can expose them to fake or harmful content.
Leaning right now: unsure, which is a perfectly honest place for an evaluator to start.

models.title: A model answer for source A
lines: Author: a bottled-water company.
Purpose: to sell more bottled water.
Vested interest: yes, they earn money if you believe tap water is unsafe.
So the source is worth reading, but it is not a fair judge, and it needs balancing with an independent source.

models.title: A model pair of questions
lines: Numerical: How many days a week do you use a phone to help with schoolwork? Choose 0, 1 to 2, 3 to 4, or 5 or more.
Narrative: Can you describe a time your phone helped or hurt your learning?
The first gives a number to show how widespread something is; the second gives a story to show what it feels like.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 3 of Global Perspectives, and the skill is Evaluation.
Ask it: In one or two sentences, how is evaluation different from research?
Then tell the tutor about one time you saw a message online that you were not sure you could believe, and ask what made you unsure.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think evaluation means.
Ask the tutor: Is my definition missing anything important, such as giving reasons?
Then ask it to give you one everyday example of evaluation that has nothing to do with school.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Write one sentence that analyses your Challenge topic and one that evaluates a source about it.
Read both to your AI tutor and ask: Which is analysis and which is evaluation, and how can you tell?
Ask the tutor to help you turn a plain judgement, such as 'this source is weak', into a full evaluation with a reason.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe to your AI tutor a surprising story or message you have seen online.
Ask it to help you list the warning signs you should look for to judge whether it is real or fake.
Ask: What is one way I could check this story before I decide to believe it?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Pick one online source about your Challenge topic and describe it to your AI tutor.
Work through the reliability checklist together, answering yes or no to each question.
Ask the tutor: Based on our answers, how reliable is this source, and what is the single biggest warning sign?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor about one source on your topic. Say who wrote it and what you think their purpose is.
Ask it: Does this author have a vested interest, something to gain if I agree with them?
Ask the tutor to suggest a second source, with nothing to gain, that could balance the first.

toolkit.title: The evaluation cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever your source or argument, good evaluation follows the same seven steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel unsure.
items: Check the source: is it real or fake? Run the reliability checklist.
Ask author and purpose: who made it, why, and do they have a vested interest?
Sort: separate the facts from the opinions.
Spot: find any bias, exaggeration or unsupported claims.
Find the argument: name the claim, the reasons and the evidence.
Weigh: list the strengths and weaknesses, and compare the two sides fairly.
Judge: reach a judgement and justify it with reasons and evidence.

toolkit.title: The Evaluation skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Evaluation is judging how trustworthy a source is and how strong an argument is, by weighing its strengths and its weaknesses, and then reaching a judgement you can support with reasons. It is not just saying you dislike something, and it is not the same as analysis, which explains why things happen.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always weigh both strengths and weaknesses, never only the faults. Second, always give a reason for every judgement, so it is never just 'this is weak' but 'this is weak because ...'. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 7 Evaluation objectives
toolkit.intro:
Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong evaluation looks like at this stage. Here are the official Evaluation objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

These are the only two Evaluation objectives at Stage 7. Everything in this unit, from spotting fake news to comparing two arguments, is a way of getting better at these two.

It helps to see how the two fit together. Objective 3.1 is about the source: is it real, reliable and fair? Objective 3.2 is about the argument inside the source: how well does it use a claim, reasons and evidence? A truly strong piece of information passes both tests, so a full evaluation usually checks 3.1 first and then 3.2.

rows: Evaluate sources, considering the author and purpose, recognising that some sources may be biased.
Judge whether a source is real, reliable and fair. Ask who made it and why, and watch for bias and vested interest.
Discuss the effectiveness of a source, making explicit reference to its development of an argument.
Judge how well a source argues its case. Find the claim, reasons and evidence, and weigh how convincing they are.

toolkit.title: Fact and opinion
toolkit.intro: Opinions are not bad, and strong arguments often include them. But keep them separate from facts, because a source that hides an opinion inside factual-sounding words is trying to slip a judgement past you.

rows: Something that can be checked and proven to be true.
Bottled water costs more than water from the public tap.
What someone thinks or believes; others may disagree.
Bottled water tastes far nicer than tap water.

toolkit.title: The parts of an argument
toolkit.intro:
An argument is a claim, its reasons, and its evidence. Use the three questions to find each part.

A strong argument has all three parts, and the evidence really does support the claim. A weak argument is missing a part, usually the evidence, or offers evidence that does not fit the claim. A good claim is always debatable, so sensible people could disagree with it.

rows: Students would learn more if they slept longer.
A study shows teenagers who sleep longer concentrate better.

toolkit.title: Template: Strengths-and-weaknesses grid
toolkit.intro:
Copy this grid to weigh any single argument. Aim to fill in at least one box on each side, then write your judgement underneath.

My overall judgement: this argument is ______, because ______.

A grid like this keeps you honest. Because it has a column for strengths and a column for weaknesses, it stops you from only attacking a source you dislike or only praising one you agree with. If a whole column is empty, look again; almost every argument has at least one point on each side.

toolkit.title: Template: Comparing two arguments
toolkit.intro:
Copy this table to compare two sides of a question. Judge both by the same rows, so the comparison is fair.

The stronger argument is ______, because ______. The strongest point on the other side is ______.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for evaluation
toolkit.intro: Use these to put your judgements into clear words. Notice that almost every one contains the word 'because', because a judgement in Global Perspectives is only complete once you have given the reason behind it.

toolkit.title: Judging a source
items: This source is reliable / unreliable, because ...
The author's purpose seems to be to ..., so ...
This source may be biased, because it has a vested interest in ...
One fact in this source is ...; one opinion is ...

toolkit.title: Weighing an argument
items: One strength of this argument is ...
One weakness of this argument is ...
The evidence does / does not support the claim, because ...
This argument is convincing / not convincing, because ...

toolkit.title: Making a judgement
items: Overall, I judge that ..., because ...
Argument A is stronger than Argument B, because ...
The strongest point on the other side is ..., but ...
Having weighed both sides, I now think ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this source reliable?
checklists.intro: Work through these questions for any source. The more answers point to 'yes', the more reliable it probably is. It is most likely that you will already have heard of the more reliable sources.
items: Has the story been reported anywhere else?
Is it also on the radio, TV or in well-known newspapers?
Have you heard of the author or organisation that published it?
Does the website itself look real and professional?
Does the web address at the very top of the page look real?
Does the story sound believable, or is it wildly dramatic?
Are there spelling or grammar mistakes?
Is the author a real, named person you can find out about?
Is there anything odd about the dates?
Is there any other evidence that supports the story?

checklists.title: Checklist: Author and purpose
checklists.intro: Every source is made by someone for a reason. Ask these before you trust it.
items: Who wrote or made this source?
Why did they make it: to inform, to persuade, to sell, or to entertain?
What do they gain if I believe them? (This is their vested interest.)
Which side do they show, and which side do they leave out?

checklists.title: Checklist: Spotting bias and exaggeration
checklists.intro: Use these questions to catch a source that is being unfair. Remember that bias is a judgement based on a personal point of view: favouring one side, or being for or against something. Spotting it does not mean throwing the source away; it means balancing it with a fairer one.
items: Does it show only one side of the issue?
Does it use extreme words like 'always', 'never', 'the worst', or 'the best'?
Does it stretch the truth to sound bigger or worse than it is? (exaggeration)
Does it make a claim with no evidence at all? (an unsupported claim)
Does it treat people who disagree as foolish, instead of answering them?

challenge.intro: Evaluation needs at least two sides to weigh, so your Challenge should be worded as a question people genuinely disagree about. A question like 'What is plastic?' cannot be evaluated; a question like 'Should our town ban plastic bags?' can.
topics: Write your Challenge as a clear question with two possible answers: 'Should ...?' or 'Is ... better than ...?'.
Write one sentence describing what someone on the 'yes' side might argue.
Write one sentence describing what someone on the 'no' side might argue.
Write down which side you lean towards right now, and remind yourself you may change your mind.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Analysis or evaluation?
activities.label: Activity 1: Analysis or evaluation?
activities.intro:
Warm up by telling the two cousins apart. Remember: analysis explains why (look for words like 'because', 'reason', 'cause'); evaluation judges how good or trustworthy something is (look for words like 'strength', 'weakness', 'reliable', 'convincing'). For each sentence, write A for analysis or E for evaluation.

Then write one sentence of your own that analyses your Challenge topic, and one that evaluates a source about it.
steps: A. One strength is that the writer gives evidence for every point.
B. This is happening because more and more people drive to work.
C. Its main weakness is that the information is out of date.
D. The sentence is unclear, so the argument is hard to follow.
E. One reason for the litter is the lack of public bins.
F. The source is not reliable, because we do not know who wrote it.

lines: Read your six answers and your two sentences to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check your answers and explain any you got wrong in a simple way.
Ask the tutor: In my own evaluation sentence, did I give a reason for my judgement?

activities.title: Real or fake? Run the reliability checklist
activities.label: Activity 3: Real or fake? Run the reliability checklist
activities.intro: Below is a described source. Judge whether it is likely to be real or fake by working through the reliability checklist. For each question, write yes, no, or not sure. Notice how a source can feel exciting and dramatic and still fail almost every reliability test; strong feelings are not evidence.
steps: Work through all ten checklist questions for this source, writing yes, no or not sure for each.
Count how many answers point to it being fake.
Write your judgement in one sentence: real or fake, and your strongest reason.
Write one thing you could do to check the story before believing it.

boxes.title: The source to judge
lines: A brightly coloured website you have never heard of posts a shocking headline: 'Miracle drink cures every illness in one day!'
There is no author's name and no date. The web address has odd extra words in it.
No newspaper, radio or TV station is reporting the story. There are several spelling mistakes.
The page ends by asking you to pay money to receive the drink 'before it sells out'.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your checklist answers and your judgement to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether it agrees, and which warning sign is the most important here.
Ask the tutor: Why is 'asking for money before it sells out' a classic sign of a fake offer?

activities.title: Author, purpose and vested interest
activities.label: Activity 4: Author, purpose and vested interest
activities.intro:
Every source is made by someone for a reason. For each source below, write who the likely author is, what their main purpose is (to inform, to persuade, to sell, or to entertain), and whether they have a vested interest.

Then write one sentence explaining why spotting a vested interest changes how much you trust a source.
steps: A. A leaflet from a company that sells bottled water, saying tap water is unsafe.
B. A report from an independent health charity comparing water sources.
C. An advert for a study app that 'guarantees top marks'.
D. A teacher's printed guide on how to revise for exams.

boxes.title: A model answer for source A
lines: Author: a bottled-water company.
Purpose: to sell more bottled water.
Vested interest: yes, they earn money if you believe tap water is unsafe.
So the source is worth reading, but it is not a fair judge, and it needs balancing with an independent source.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check which sources have a vested interest and which are more independent.
Ask the tutor: For my own Challenge topic, which source that I am using has the strongest vested interest?

activities.title: Fact or opinion?
activities.label: Activity 5: Fact or opinion?
activities.intro:
A strong evaluator keeps facts and opinions apart. A fact can be checked and proven; an opinion is what someone thinks. For each statement, write F for fact or O for opinion.

Then find a source about your own Challenge topic and copy out one fact and one opinion from it.
steps: A. Our town gets less rain during the dry season.
B. The dry season is the most miserable time of the year.
C. Most classrooms at our school have electric lights.
D. Everyone knows that fruit is the only food worth eating.
E. A litre of bottled water costs more than a litre from the public tap.
F. Plastic bags are the worst invention in history.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers and your two examples to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check your sorting and explain any you found tricky.
Ask the tutor: How can I tell when a strong opinion is being written to sound like a fact?

activities.title: Spot the bias and exaggeration
activities.label: Activity 6: Spot the bias and exaggeration
activities.intro: Read the short, one-sided passage below. Your job is to find where it is unfair. Bias leans to one side; exaggeration stretches the truth; an unsupported claim gives no evidence. A passage can be about a real problem and still be unfair in the way it argues, and part of evaluation is separating the true worry from the unfair wording.
steps: Find two examples of exaggeration in the passage.
Find one claim that is given with no evidence at all.
Explain in one sentence how the passage treats people who disagree.
Rewrite the first sentence in a fair, balanced way that an evaluator could trust.

boxes.title: The passage to judge
lines: Everybody knows that plastic bags are completely destroying our beautiful town. They are the single worst thing on the planet, and only a foolish person would ever defend them.
Our brilliant clean-up group is the only group that truly cares. No sensible reason exists to keep using bags, and anyone who disagrees simply has not thought about it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your findings and your fair rewrite to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you caught the main examples of bias and exaggeration.
Ask the tutor: Does my rewrite still make a point, but in a fair way?

activities.title: Find the argument
activities.label: Activity 7: Find the argument
activities.intro:
An argument has three parts: a claim (what the author thinks), a reason (why), and evidence (how they know). Read the passage and pull out all three. Remember the three questions that unlock them: the claim answers 'What do I think?', the reason answers 'Why do I think this?', and the evidence answers 'How do I know this?'.

Then find a short argument about your own Challenge topic and label its claim, reason and evidence in the same way.
steps: Write out the claim.
Write out the reason.
Write out the evidence.
Decide whether the evidence really supports the claim, and write one sentence saying why or why not.

boxes.title: The passage
lines: Our school should provide free drinking water at every classroom. Students would concentrate better in the afternoon heat, because a recent school survey found that two out of three students said they feel thirsty and tired by the last lesson of the day.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your three labelled parts to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check whether you found the claim, reason and evidence correctly.
Ask the tutor: Is any part missing from my own topic's argument, and how does that weaken it?

activities.title: Write and test a claim
activities.label: Activity 8: Write and test a claim
activities.intro: Now make your own claim about your Challenge topic and test it, the way an evaluator would. Remember a claim must be debatable, so start with 'I believe ...'.
steps: Write one debatable claim about your topic, beginning 'I believe ...'.
Write three questions that would test your claim, such as 'What evidence is there?' and 'Who might disagree?'.
Write the strongest point someone on the other side could make.
Decide whether your claim survived the test, and adjust it if it did not.

boxes.title: What makes a claim worth testing
lines: It is debatable, so sensible people could take different sides.
It is clear, so everyone understands exactly what is being claimed.
It is about your topic, not a side issue.
It can be checked against real evidence, not just feelings.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your claim, your test questions and the other side's strongest point to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your claim is genuinely debatable and clear.
Ask the tutor to play the other side and argue against your claim, so you can see how it holds up.

activities.title: Numerical and narrative evidence
activities.label: Activity 9: Numerical and narrative evidence
activities.intro:
Evidence comes in two types. Numerical evidence comes from closed questions that give numbers or a yes/no answer. Narrative evidence comes from open questions that give a fuller story. For each survey question below, write N for numerical or R for narrative.

Then write two survey questions about your Challenge topic: one that would give numerical evidence and one that would give narrative evidence.
steps: A. Do you own a mobile phone? Yes or no.
B. Why do you think students use their phones during lessons?
C. How many hours a day do you spend on a phone? Choose from a list.
D. How does using a phone at night affect your sleep, in your own words?

boxes.title: A model pair of questions
lines: Numerical: How many days a week do you use a phone to help with schoolwork? Choose 0, 1 to 2, 3 to 4, or 5 or more.
Narrative: Can you describe a time your phone helped or hurt your learning?
The first gives a number to show how widespread something is; the second gives a story to show what it feels like.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four answers and your two new questions to your AI tutor.
Ask it to check whether your two questions really give numerical and narrative evidence.
Ask the tutor: For my claim, which type of evidence would be more convincing, and why?

activities.title: Compare two arguments and make a judgement
activities.label: Activity 10: Compare two arguments and make a judgement
activities.intro: This is where everything comes together. Find, or imagine, two short arguments on opposite sides of your Challenge question. Judge both by the same questions, then decide which is stronger. This is the exact skill Cambridge means by objective 3.2: discussing how effectively a source develops its argument.
steps: Write a one-line summary of Argument A and Argument B.
For each argument, write one strength and one weakness.
Note whether either source has a vested interest.
Write your judgement: which argument is stronger, your main reason, and the strongest point on the other side.

boxes.title: Keep your comparison fair
lines: Judge both arguments by the same set of questions.
Do not be harder on the side you already disagree with.
Look for at least one strength and one weakness in each.
End with a judgement that rests on a reason, not just a feeling.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your comparison and your final judgement to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you judged both arguments fairly and by the same questions.
Ask the tutor: Have I been fair to the side I disagree with, and is my judgement backed by a reason?

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your comparison of the two arguments and your justified judgement.
Share them in your next teacher session, and listen for a classmate who judged the same sources differently.
Ask yourself: did hearing another view change my judgement, or make my reasons stronger?

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Try every question before you look at the answer key, and give your own words rather than copying from the other files. As you answer, remember the two habits that run through the whole unit: weigh both strengths and weaknesses, and give a reason for every judgement. A question that asks you to judge something is really asking for those two things.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does 'evaluation' mean?
practice.answer: Evaluation means judging how trustworthy a source is and how strong an argument is, weighing strengths and weaknesses, and reaching a judgement backed by reasons. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: What is the main difference between analysis and evaluation?
practice.answer: Analysis explains why things happen; evaluation judges how good, strong or trustworthy something is.

practice.prompt: True or false: to evaluate a source you should give only its weaknesses.
practice.answer: False. A fair evaluation gives both strengths and weaknesses.

practice.prompt: What is 'fake news'?
practice.answer: Fake news is a story that is invented or twisted but made to look like a real report so people believe and share it.

practice.prompt: Name two questions from the reliability checklist you would ask about a source.
practice.answer: Any two of: Has it been reported elsewhere? Is it on radio, TV or in newspapers? Have you heard of the author or organisation? Does the website and its address look real? Does it sound believable? Are there spelling mistakes? Is the author a real person? Is anything odd about the dates? Is there other evidence?

practice.prompt: A source made by someone who has something to gain if you believe it has a ______ interest.
practice.answer: Vested interest.

practice.prompt: What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
practice.answer: A fact can be checked and proven to be true; an opinion is what someone thinks and others may disagree with.

practice.prompt: Name the three parts of an argument.
practice.answer: A claim, the reasons for it, and the evidence that supports it.

practice.prompt: The claim answers 'What do I think?'. What question does the evidence answer?
practice.answer: It answers 'How do I know this?'

practice.prompt: A good claim must be ______, which means people could reasonably disagree with it.
practice.answer: Debatable.

practice.prompt: Evidence from a closed question that gives numbers is called ______ evidence.
practice.answer: Numerical evidence.

practice.prompt: Evidence from an open question that gives a fuller story is called ______ evidence.
practice.answer: Narrative evidence.

practice.prompt: When you weigh an argument, you should look for both its strengths and its ______.
practice.answer: Weaknesses.

practice.prompt: Stretching the truth to make something sound bigger or worse than it is, is called ______.
practice.answer: Exaggeration.

practice.prompt: Give one reason why you should note the strongest point on the other side when you make a judgement.
practice.answer: Any one of: it shows you judged fairly; it makes your judgement more trustworthy; it proves you weighed both sides, not just the one you agreed with.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each evaluation word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Bias
options: A. Anything that backs up a claim, such as a survey, report or study.
B. A debatable statement that an author wants you to accept.
C. When a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
D. A source that can be trusted to be true.
E. Something that can be checked and proven to be true.
F. When the person behind a source has something to gain if you believe it.
practice.answer: C — When a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Vested interest
practice.answer: F — When the person behind a source has something to gain if you believe it.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Claim
practice.answer: B — A debatable statement that an author wants you to accept.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: A — Anything that backs up a claim, such as a survey, report or study.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Reliable source
practice.answer: D — A source that can be trusted to be true.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Fact
practice.answer: E — Something that can be checked and proven to be true.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each. In every answer, try to name the evaluation idea you are using, such as vested interest, bias, fact and opinion, or real and fake, so you can see the skill behind your judgement.
practice.prompt: Zara sees a shocking story on a website she has never heard of, reported nowhere else. Should she share it straight away? Why or why not?
practice.answer: No. It is on an unknown website and reported nowhere else, which are warning signs. She should check a trusted source before sharing.

practice.prompt: Karim reads a leaflet praising plastic bags, written by a company that sells them. How should the company's vested interest change how much he trusts it?
practice.answer: The company gains if he believes the leaflet, so it is a biased, one-sided source. He should trust it less and balance it with an independent source.

practice.prompt: Nadia reads: 'The school serves rice four days a week, which is clearly a terrible diet.' Which part is fact and which is opinion?
practice.answer: Fact: the school serves rice four days a week. Opinion: that this is a 'terrible diet'.

practice.prompt: Omar finds an advert that says a lamp is 'the best in the whole world' with no evidence. Name the two problems with that sentence.
practice.answer: It is an exaggeration ('the best in the whole world') and an unsupported claim (no evidence is given).

practice.prompt: Tariq has two articles about phones: one from a phone shop, one from an independent charity. If both make similar points, which is the fairer judge, and why?
practice.answer: The independent charity is the fairer judge, because it has no vested interest, while the phone shop gains if you agree with it.

reflection.prompt: Working on my own, at my own pace ...
Working with my AI tutor, my discussion partner ...

vocabulary.meaning: Judging how trustworthy a source is and how strong an argument is, and giving reasons.
Breaking a topic into parts and explaining why things happen.
Anywhere your information comes from: a website, book, video, person or message.
Able to be trusted to be true.
Not able to be trusted to be true.
A story that is invented or twisted but made to look like a real report.
The person or group who made a source.
The reason a source was made: to inform, persuade, sell or entertain.
When the person behind a source has something to gain if you believe it.
A judgement based on a personal point of view; unfairly favouring one side.
Stretching the truth to make something sound bigger or worse than it is.
A statement given with no evidence to back it up.
Something that can be checked and proven to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others may disagree with.
A claim, the reasons for it, and the evidence that supports it.
A debatable statement that an author wants you to accept.
Able to be argued about, because sensible people could disagree.
Why an author holds a claim; it answers the question 'Why do I think this?'.
Anything that backs up a claim, such as a survey, report or study.
Genuinely related to the topic or claim being explored.
Evidence from closed questions that give numbers or a yes/no answer.
Evidence from open questions that give a fuller story in someone's own words.
Something an argument or source does well.
Something an argument or source does badly, or leaves out.
Working well; an effective argument is clear and convincing.
Strong enough in reasons and evidence to make you believe it.
A clear, reasoned decision about a source or an argument.
To give the reasons and evidence behind a judgement.
To check a claim against evidence and other people to see if it holds up.

mistakes: Giving a judgement with no reason, so it is really just an opinion.
Listing only weaknesses, or only strengths, instead of weighing both.
Believing or sharing a dramatic story before checking whether it is real.
Trusting a source without asking who wrote it and why.
Missing a vested interest, and treating a seller's advert as a fair judge.
Being harder on the side you already disagree with.
Confusing analysis (explaining why) with evaluation (judging how strong).

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does 'evaluation' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaluation means judging how trustworthy a source is and how strong an argument is, weighing strengths and weaknesses, and reaching a judgement backed by reasons. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: What is the main difference between analysis and evaluation?
questions.modelAnswer: Analysis explains why things happen; evaluation judges how good, strong or trustworthy something is.

questions.prompt: True or false: to evaluate a source you should give only its weaknesses.
questions.modelAnswer: False. A fair evaluation gives both strengths and weaknesses.
Fake news is a story that is invented or twisted but made to look like a real report so people believe and share it.

questions.prompt: Name two questions from the reliability checklist you would ask about a source.
questions.modelAnswer: Any two of: Has it been reported elsewhere? Is it on radio, TV or in newspapers? Have you heard of the author or organisation? Does the website and its address look real? Does it sound believable? Are there spelling mistakes? Is the author a real person? Is anything odd about the dates? Is there other evidence?

questions.prompt: A source made by someone who has something to gain if you believe it has a ______ interest.
What is the difference between a fact and an opinion?
questions.modelAnswer: A fact can be checked and proven to be true; an opinion is what someone thinks and others may disagree with.

questions.prompt: Name the three parts of an argument.
questions.modelAnswer: A claim, the reasons for it, and the evidence that supports it.

questions.prompt: The claim answers 'What do I think?'. What question does the evidence answer?
questions.modelAnswer: It answers 'How do I know this?'

questions.prompt: A good claim must be ______, which means people could reasonably disagree with it.
Evidence from a closed question that gives numbers is called ______ evidence.
Evidence from an open question that gives a fuller story is called ______ evidence.

selfAssessment.statement: I understand what the word 'evaluation' means.
I can explain the difference between analysis and evaluation.
I can judge whether an information source is likely to be real or fake.
I can evaluate a source by its author and purpose, and spot a vested interest.
I can tell the difference between a fact and an opinion.
I can spot bias, exaggeration and claims given with no evidence.
I can find the claim, reasons and evidence in an argument.
I can weigh the strengths and weaknesses of an argument.
I can compare two arguments and make a judgement I can justify.
